subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: establishing the facts before acting [Thinking]
passage:
Come, Sahil, sit. You've told me the figures in one client's file look too big to you. Let me tell you what I did once. I'm Disha.
I was an analyst, junior like you, and a client report showed a total higher than its own parts. My stomach turned. I wanted to run to my manager and say someone had cooked the numbers.
Instead I re-added every line myself, and traced each figure to its source file. Then I made two lists. What I know: one region's sales had been counted twice. What I suspect: that it was deliberate. I had no proof of that.
Then I asked Ganesh, who assembled the sheet, to walk me through it. Ganesh went pale, then said, "I copied the region twice by mistake."
Facts first, then questions. That order saved us both.

qa.q: What was counted twice in the report?
qa.a: One region's sales had been counted twice.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling on seeing the total higher than its parts?
qa.a: Disha felt alarm and a strong urge to accuse, since Disha's stomach turned and Disha wanted to run to the manager.

qa.q: Disha re-added the lines and made a list of what was known and what was suspected. What did that choice help with?
qa.a: It kept the known error apart from an unproven guess, so Disha did not accuse anyone without proof.

qa.q: How might Ganesh have felt when asked to walk through the sheet?
qa.a: Ganesh was probably nervous and afraid of being blamed, as going pale shows, but answered honestly.

grounding: The elder's story shows an analyst who, on spotting inflated numbers, rechecks calculations and sources and separates what is known from what is suspected before accusing anyone.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: establishing the facts before acting [Thinking]

The client deck was due at six, and at four Binita noticed the growth figure on slide nine: 38 percent. Her own data pull last week had shown 21. Kamal, the account lead, had finalised the slides that morning.
Her first instinct was to message the team: 'Who inflated this?' She didn't. She reopened the source files and rebuilt the calculation step by step. The raw sales data said 21. She checked the other slides; two more numbers were higher than the source.
On a notepad she drew a line down the middle. Left side, KNOWN: slide 9 says 38, source says 21; slides 12 and 14 also differ. Right side, SUSPECTED: changed on purpose? A different data version?
At 4.40 she went to Kamal's desk with the notepad and the source files, and asked which version he had used.

qa.q: What growth figure did Binita's own data pull show?
Why didn't Binita message the team, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She was alarmed and suspicious, but careful not to accuse anyone before knowing whether the numbers were changed on purpose.

qa.q: What could Binita do next if Kamal can't explain the numbers?
qa.a: She could hold the deck, keep her notes of the known facts and follow the company's process to raise it with someone senior.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel when Binita shows him the notepad?
qa.a: Kamal might feel defensive or embarrassed, but being asked which version he used gives him room to explain or correct it.

grounding: It shows an analyst who notices inflated numbers re-checking the source and separating known facts from suspicion before speaking to anyone.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: establishing the facts before acting [Thinking]
passage:
In the Gurugram office, after everyone had left, Zeenat sat with the market survey report Anirban had sent her to proofread. The summary said 2,400 respondents. The data file she had cleaned herself had 1,650.
She spoke under her breath as she worked. 'Okay. What do I actually know?' She counted rows again: 1,650. She searched the shared drive and found an older draft with duplicates: 2,400 rows. 'So either he used the wrong file, or he chose the bigger number.' She wrote both possibilities down and circled the first. 'I don't know which. I only know the report doesn't match the clean data.'
She saved screenshots of both files with their dates, then wrote Anirban a short note asking to go through the numbers together at ten the next morning.

qa.q: How many rows did the clean data file have?
What does Zeenat circling the first possibility suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels uneasy but wants to be fair, giving Anirban the benefit of the doubt until she knows more.

qa.q: Which other approach might have gone badly here, and why?
qa.a: Forwarding the report to the manager with an accusation would claim something she hasn't proven and could damage trust if it was an honest file mix-up.

qa.q: How might Anirban see the note asking to meet at ten?
qa.a: A calm request to go through the numbers lets Anirban explain or correct the file, rather than feel ambushed.

grounding: It shows an analyst who spots inflated figures in a client report re-checking the source and separating what is known from what is suspected.
